coverage_gaps: Need primary-source verification from the latest 10-K/10-Q filings and earnings calls of hyperscalers for capex, depreciation, AI infrastructure commitments, and capacity constraints.
Need company-level capacity evidence for HBM vendors, advanced packaging capacity, substrate suppliers, and OSATs rather than relying only on secondary market commentary.
Need a broader non-U.S. public-market mapping: Taiwan, Korea, Japan, Europe, and A-share suppliers may control important memory, substrate, equipment, optical, and power-infrastructure nodes.
Need separation of training demand versus inference demand because the supply-chain mix differs across GPUs/ASICs, memory, networking, storage, and software.
Need market-pricing checks for each node: revenue growth already priced, valuation multiples, backlog visibility, cyclicality, and customer concentration.
Need falsification indicators: hyperscaler capex cuts, lower model-scaling intensity, falling accelerator utilization, HBM oversupply, delayed data-center energization, or weak enterprise AI ROI.

evidence.claim: The IEA reported that large technology companies' capital expenditure exceeded USD 400 billion in 2025 and was expected to rise by another 75% in 2026, while global data-center electricity demand grew 17% in 2025.
evidence.source_title: Key Questions on Energy and AI - Executive Summary

evidence.claim: Epoch AI found that in 2025 the four largest AI chip designers consumed over 90% of global CoWoS packaging capacity and HBM supply by value, but only about 12% of advanced logic die production, implying packaging and HBM were the primary AI chip supply constraints.
evidence.source_title: Advanced packaging and HBM, not logic dies, were the bottlenecks on AI chip production in 2025

evidence.claim: TrendForce reported that North American AI data-center expansion was driving 2026 capex of the top nine cloud service providers to US$830 billion.
evidence.source_title: North American AI Data Center Expansion Drives 2026 CapEx of Top Nine CSPs to US$830 Billion, Says TrendForce

evidence.claim: Stanford HAI's 2026 AI Index reported broad organizational AI adoption and rapid generative AI adoption, supporting the software automation demand leg of the theme.
Recent industry reporting highlights photonics and high-speed data movement as an emerging AI infrastructure bottleneck after constraints in copper, power, DRAM, and NAND.
evidence.source_title: Photonics and high-speed data movement is the next big AI bottleneck

evidence.claim: Academic research on U.S. hyperscale data centers estimated that hyperscale data-center electricity demand under a central scenario corresponded to about 1.8% of total U.S. electricity consumption for facilities operating between May 2024 and April 2025.
evidence.source_title: Assessing the Carbon Emissions and Energy Consumption of U.S. Hyperscale Data Centers

memory_update.text: AI theme should be tracked as an infrastructure-plus-automation funnel: hyperscaler capex drives compute, networking, data-center infrastructure, power, and software monetization layers.
HBM plus advanced packaging is a high-priority AI chokepoint because it can constrain accelerator supply even when leading-edge logic wafer capacity is available.
Data-center power, cooling, grid interconnection, transformers, switchgear, and construction labor are durable physical bottlenecks for AI deployment.
AI networking and optical interconnect should be treated as a separate scarce layer, not just as a derivative of GPU demand.
Enterprise AI software exposure should be evaluated through production deployment, governed data access, workflow integration, security, and measurable ROI rather than generic AI branding.

Next funnel layer should build a public-company universe across U.S., Taiwan, Korea, Japan, Europe, and China A-shares for each AI supply-chain node, then score bottleneck control and evidence quality.

summary: AI is best decomposed as a multi-layer infrastructure and automation supercycle rather than a single semiconductor trade. The highest-quality first-pass funnel should track: hyperscaler capex as the primary demand signal; accelerator plus HBM plus advanced packaging as the core compute bottleneck; networking and optical interconnect as the cluster-scaling bottleneck; power, cooling, grid interconnection, and site delivery as the physical infrastructure bottleneck; energy procurement and firm capacity as second-order constraints; and enterprise software/data-governance layers as the monetization and automation layer. This is research support only and does not provide buy/sell recommendations.

supply_chain_nodes.bottleneck_hypothesis: The real constraint is a combined HBM plus advanced packaging bottleneck rather than pure leading-edge wafer capacity. Suppliers with access to HBM allocation, CoWoS/2.5D capacity, and packaging yield learning may control a disproportionate share of AI compute output.

demand_drivers: Hyperscaler AI infrastructure capex for model training, inference, and cloud AI services.
Enterprise adoption of generative AI and agentic workflow automation across business functions.
Sovereign AI and private-cloud buildouts by governments, regulated industries, and large enterprises.
Rising inference demand from consumer AI, software copilots, search, advertising, coding, contact-center, and productivity workflows.

theme_map.public_market_search_strategy: Start with the broad AI spend pool, then map scarce layers before mapping tickers. Search in stages: (1) hyperscaler capex and data-center buildout disclosures; (2) HBM, advanced packaging, and foundry capacity evidence; (3) AI networking, optical modules, and silicon photonics roadmaps; (4) data-center power, cooling, grid, and energy procurement constraints; (5) software automation adoption, enterprise AI deployment, and data-governance bottlenecks. Use the pilot universe as seed exposure, but expand to memory makers, OSATs, EDA, semiconductor equipment, optical component suppliers, electrical equipment, cooling, EPC/grid contractors, utilities, independent power producers, and enterprise software/data platforms.
supply_side_constraints: HBM supply, CoWoS/advanced packaging capacity, and yield/qualification timelines.
Leading-edge foundry capacity and semiconductor equipment availability, especially lithography, etch, deposition, inspection, and packaging tools.
800G/1.6T networking, switch silicon, optical modules, silicon photonics, co-packaged optics, and fiber supply for large AI clusters.
Data-center power availability, grid interconnection queues, transformers, switchgear, backup generation, and electrical labor.
Thermal density constraints from liquid cooling, heat rejection, water availability, and site-level engineering.
Enterprise data integration, security, workflow orchestration, observability, and governance needed to move AI from pilots to production.
